patterns.skill: Before any ALTER TABLE: capture with execute_sql('CREATE TABLE <backup_name> AS SELECT * FROM <table_name>'). For additive changes (ADD COLUMN, ADD CONSTRAINT, RENAME TO/COLUMN), reverse with the inverse DDL — no capture needed but having it is harmless. For destructive changes (DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN TYPE): restore from backup using execute_sql with multi-statement SQL: ADD the lost column(s) back matching the backup table's column definition, UPDATE data FROM backup via the primary key, then DROP the backup table. The backup table preserves both schema and data, making get_object_details unnecessary.
patterns.verify_note: Tested two ALTER TABLE variants on throwaway table chats_probe_alter_test: (1) ADD COLUMN phone text -> reversed with DROP COLUMN phone — cheap inverse works, no capture needed. (2) DROP COLUMN status — destructive. get_object_details alone is insufficient (only captures schema, not row data). Verified capture-and-restore: CREATE TABLE backup AS SELECT * -> DROP COLUMN -> ADD COLUMN + UPDATE FROM backup restored all 3 rows with id/name/status intact (alpha/active, beta/active, gamma/inactive). This execute_sql-only approach works for all destructive ALTERs (DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN TYPE). For additive ALTERs (ADD COLUMN, ADD CONSTRAINT, RENAME) the inverse DDL suffices and the capture is harmless overhead.
patterns.recipe:
Capture: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE>'})
Restore (destructive DROP COLUMN): execute_sql({sql: 'ALTER TABLE <TABLE> ADD COLUMN <COL> <TYPE>; UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <COL> = b.<COL> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK_COL> = b.<PK_COL>; DROP TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE>'})
Restore (non-destructive ADD COLUMN): execute_sql({sql: 'ALTER TABLE <TABLE> DROP COLUMN <COL>'})

skill:
How to back up mutations on the "postgres" server — every entry was VERIFIED live and is the fewest-calls recipe found; follow it VERBATIM, do not explore for alternatives.

SHARED DISCOVERY CALL — one call that finds AND dumps whatever hangs off the table. Run it before any row-removing or table-changing action; it returns nothing when there is nothing to find, so run it unconditionally:
execute_sql({sql: "SELECT pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid)||E'\n'||pg_get_functiondef(p.oid) FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=t.tgrelid JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid=t.tgfoid WHERE NOT t.tgisinternal AND c.oid='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass UNION ALL SELECT c.oid::regclass::text||E'\n'||query_to_xml('SELECT * FROM ONLY '||c.oid::regclass::text,true,false,'')::text FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass;"})
It returns each non-internal trigger with its function body, AND one row per INHERITS child carrying that child's FULL rows via query_to_xml — including the child's own extra columns, which a SELECT * on the parent silently drops. Capture every table named in the returned trigger function bodies too.
When the action can cascade through foreign keys, one more call:
execute_sql({sql: "SELECT conrelid::regclass AS child, confdeltype FROM pg_constraint WHERE confrelid='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass AND contype='f';"})

- insert (trigger: insert): The INSERT that creates the row MUST include RETURNING id (or the primary key). Capture the returned id. Reverse with execute_sql({sql: 'DELETE FROM <TABLE> WHERE <PK_COLUMN> = <CAPTURED_ID>;'}). One call creates + captures the pin; one call reverses. Capture nothing else — the id is the only pin needed.
- update (trigger: update): CAPTURE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE> WHERE <the UPDATE's own WHERE>;'}) — let the database make the copy; NEVER select the rows into your own context. Verify with aggregates only, BOTH SIDES in one row: execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the same predicate>) AS src, (SELECT count(*) FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>) AS bak;'}) — a count of the backup alone cannot tell you a wrong predicate or a missing ONLY dropped rows. The result is one row whatever the table size. RESTORE: execute_sql({sql: 'INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>;'}), or UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <col> = b.<col> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK> = b.<PK>. Then note what you backed up and where it went.
- delete (trigger: delete): CAPTURE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE> WHERE <THE DELETE'S OWN WHERE>;'}) — let the database make the copy; NEVER select the rows into your own context. Verify with aggregates only, BOTH SIDES in one row: execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the same predicate>) AS src, (SELECT count(*) FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>) AS bak;'}) — a count of the backup alone cannot tell you a wrong predicate or a missing ONLY dropped rows. The result is one row whatever the table size. RESTORE: execute_sql({sql: 'INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>;'}). Then note what you backed up and where it went. Do the same for every child the SHARED DISCOVERY CALL reports, one backup table each.
- truncate (trigger: truncate): CAPTURE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE>;'}) — let the database make the copy; NEVER select the rows into your own context. Verify with aggregates only, BOTH SIDES in one row: execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the same predicate>) AS src, (SELECT count(*) FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>) AS bak;'}) — a count of the backup alone cannot tell you a wrong predicate or a missing ONLY dropped rows. The result is one row whatever the table size. RESTORE: execute_sql({sql: 'INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>;'}). Then note what you backed up and where it went. Do the same for every child, restore parent first.
- drop (trigger: drop): Before any DROP (TABLE, VIEW), capture in THREE calls: (1) get_object_details(schema_name, object_name, 'table') for structure — columns, defaults, PK, indexes; (2) execute_sql({sql: "CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE>;\nSELECT viewname, pg_get_viewdef(viewname, true) FROM pg_views WHERE schemaname = '<SCHEMA>' AND viewname IN (SELECT dependent_view.relname FROM pg_depend JOIN pg_rewrite ON pg_depend.objid = pg_rewrite.oid JOIN pg_class AS dependent_view ON pg_rewrite.ev_class = dependent_view.oid WHERE pg_depend.refobjid = '<TABLE>'::regclass AND pg_depend.classid = 'pg_rewrite'::regclass);\nSELECT sequencename, last_value, is_called FROM pg_sequences WHERE schemaname = '<SCHEMA>' AND sequencename LIKE '<TABLE>%';"}) — rows, dependent view definitions, and owned sequence state in one multi-statement call; (3) the SHARED DISCOVERY CALL, because the probe this recipe was verified against had dependent VIEWS and a sequence but NO inheritance, so children were never exercised. RESTORE with ONE execute_sql combining, in order: CREATE TABLE <SCHEMA>.<TABLE> from the captured columns, defaults and constraints; INSERT all rows with explicit ids so foreign keys still resolve; SELECT setval() per captured sequence; CREATE VIEW per captured dependent view; and one INSERT per inheritance child. That preserves id stability, sequence continuity and dependent objects.
- alter (trigger: alter): Before any ALTER TABLE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE>'}) — the backup table holds both schema and data, which makes get_object_details unnecessary here. RESTORE after a destructive DROP COLUMN: execute_sql({sql: 'ALTER TABLE <TABLE> ADD COLUMN <COL> <TYPE>; UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <COL> = b.<COL> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK_COL> = b.<PK_COL>; DROP TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE>'}). RESTORE after a non-destructive ADD COLUMN: execute_sql({sql: 'ALTER TABLE <TABLE> DROP COLUMN <COL>'}).
- create (trigger: create): Before CREATE, confirm the object does not exist; after, DROP the created object to restore prior state.

PRE-STATE CAPTURE — copy INSIDE the database first. execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the action's own predicate>'}); record <BACKUP_TABLE> as the artifact. RESTORE: UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <col> = b.<col> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK> = b.<PK> (or INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> for deleted rows). The rows never enter your context, so their size does not matter.
